query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a high-temperature sliding environment, adding a controlled amount of nano-CeO2 to the FeNiCrCoCu coating refines its grain structure and promotes the formation of a stable, continuous oxide layer at grain boundaries that retards dislocation motion, thereby reducing microscopic plastic deformation and overall wear compared to the baseline coating with no CeO2.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with its baseline microstructure (as obtained by the standard deposition process without additional modifying agents).
generation.intervention: Add a controlled quantity of nano-CeO2 particles to the alloy powder feed during the coating process.
generation.conditions: The coating is processed under the same deposition conditions as the baseline, then subjected to high-temperature sliding wear tests in an oxidizing environment (with controlled load, sliding speed, and temperature parameters as defined by the application regime).
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure with enhanced and continuous Ce-enriched oxide films at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Nano-CeO2 particles serve as nucleation sites during solidification, leading to finer grains and more pinned grain boundaries. Under high-temperature sliding, these sites facilitate the formation and stabilization of a protective oxide tribo-layer that impedes dislocation movement and microcrack initiation, thereby improving wear resistance and reducing plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The primary measurement—wear rate—will be lower, and microscopic examination will show reduced evidence of plastic deformation (e.g., fewer micro-cracks and less plastic flow) compared to the baseline coating.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating prepared without the nano-CeO2 additive.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic improvement is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions in an oxidizing environment where tribo-oxidation plays a significant role in surface protection.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in wear rate and degree of microstructural refinement depend on the precise CeO2 content and processing parameters, which remain to be optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one group with the predetermined nano-CeO2 additive and one group without (baseline). Subject both groups to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests under controlled load, speed, and temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate via mass loss or wear track volume measurements
Microscopic analysis (SEM/EDS) of the surface and subsurface to evaluate grain size, presence of protective oxide layers, and signs of plastic deformation
Tribological performance metrics such as friction coefficient
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nano-CeO2-modified coatings do not display a statistically significant decrease in wear rate and exhibit similar or increased levels of microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

The SEM was used to scan the microscopic morphology of different regions of the three coatings [,]. Figure 5 shows the microstructure of the three coatings at the top, middle, and bottom, respectively. As can be seen from Figure 5a–c, the top microstructure of the HEA coating was mainly composed of flocculent grains; the microstructure in the middle of the coating was reticular, and the grain grew directionally; the bottom of the coating was mainly composed of reticular grains, but dendritic grains also appeared, which were the result of the reaction among five principal elements in the coating during the cladding process and the formation of trace metal compounds after cooling []. There were no defects in the HEA coating, such as pores and cracks []. As can be seen from Figure 5d–f, with the addition of WC content, the grain morphology also changed due to the change of phase, and secondary crystal axis began to be formed.
